chunks.text: 2 Method Problem Statement. In the CA setting, we consider two datasets X = { x i } i = 1 N X=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and Y = { y j } j = 1 M Y=\{y_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} . Most prior work adopts a background-target (BT) assumption, where only one dataset (typically Y Y ) contains a dataset-specific (or salient ) pattern (e.g., a pathology) absent from the other, while both share common content (e.g., healthy anatomy). We generalize CA to a multiple-salient (MS) setting, where both X X and Y Y contain their own salient patterns that are absent in the other. Our goal is to learn a common generative factor c ∈ ℝ d c c\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{c}} capturing information shared across X X and Y Y , and salient generative factors s x ∈ ℝ d s ​ x s_{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{sx}} , s y ∈ ℝ d s ​ y s_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{sy}} that capture variations unique to X X and Y Y , respectively. Common and Salient (CS)-StyleGAN. In the context of StyleGAN, given samples x ∈ X x\in X and y ∈ Y y\in Y , an encoder E E (i.e., pSp [ 26 ] ) maps them to latent codes w x = E ⁡ ( x ) w_{x}=E(x) and w y = E ⁡ ( y ) w_{y}=E(y) , where w x , w y ∈ ℝ d w w_{x},w_{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{w}} . We introduce a CS separator H cs , ϕ H_{\mathrm{cs},\phi} , which consists of one common branch 𝒞 ϕ c \mathcal{C}_{\phi_{c}} and two salient branches 𝒮 x , ϕ s ​ x \mathcal{S}_{x,\phi_{sx}} and 𝒮 y , ϕ s ​ y \mathcal{S}_{y,\phi_{sy}} . For brevity, we omit the parameters ϕ \phi in the following. We define the latent factors as: c x = 𝒞 ⁡ ( w x ) c_{x}=\mathcal{C}(w_{x}) and c y = 𝒞 ⁡ ( w y ) c_{y}=\mathcal{C}(w_{y}) . In the MS setting, we set s x = 𝒮 x ​ ( w x ) s_{x}=\mathcal{S}_{x}(w_{x}) and s y = 𝒮 y ​ ( w y ) s_{y}=\mathcal{S}_{y}(w_{y}) , while in the BT setting, we remove 𝒮 x \mathcal{S}_{x} and use 𝒮 y \mathcal{S}_{y} only (all 𝒮 x \mathcal{S}_{x} -related terms are omitted). Latent Regularization.

We first train the H c ​ s H_{cs} separator with the following reconstruction loss in the StyleGAN2 latent space: ℒ lat = ‖ 𝒞 ⁡ ( w x ) + 𝒮 x ​ ( w x ) − w x ‖ 2 2 + ‖ 𝒞 ⁡ ( w y ) + 𝒮 y ​ ( w y ) − w y ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\text{lat}}=\|\mathcal{C}(w_{x})+\mathcal{S}_{x}(w_{x})-w_{x}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\mathcal{C}(w_{y})+\mathcal{S}_{y}(w_{y})-w_{y}\|_{2}^{2}, (1) where each term encourages the sum of the common output and the corresponding salient output to reconstruct the StyleGAN2 latent ( w x w_{x} or w y w_{y} ). To enforce that the salient factors capture only dataset-specific information, we additionally penalize cross-dataset activations, by minimizing ‖ 𝒮 y ​ ( w x ) ‖ 2 2 \|\mathcal{S}_{y}(w_{x})\|_{2}^{2} and ‖ 𝒮 x ​ ( w y ) ‖ 2 2 \|\mathcal{S}_{x}(w_{y})\|_{2}^{2} (we use only ‖ 𝒮 y ​ ( w x ) ‖ 2 2 \|\mathcal{S}_{y}(w_{x})\|_{2}^{2} under the BT assumption, as explained in Fig. 1 ). The loss in Eq. ( 1 ) is necessary but insufficient. In particular, it does not enforce (i) common consistency , i.e., that the common factors capture the same information across X X and Y Y , nor (ii) common-salient independence , i.e., that common and salient factors do not share information. To promote common consistency , we impose distributional alignment of the common factors by introducing a discriminator 𝒟 \mathcal{D} that predicts whether 𝒞 ⁡ ( w ) \mathcal{C}(w) originates from X X or Y Y , while the separator H cs H_{\mathrm{cs}} is trained to make this prediction impossible: ℒ D = min H cs ⁡ max 𝒟 ⁡ ( − 𝔼 w y ​ [ log ⁡ 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝒞 ⁡ ( w y ) ) ] − 𝔼 w x ​ [ log ⁡ ( 1 − 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝒞 ⁡ ( w x ) ) ) ] ) . \mathcal{L}_{D}=\min_{H_{\mathrm{cs}}}\max_{\mathcal{D}}\Big(-\mathbb{E}_{w_{y}}[\log\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{C}(w_{y}))]-\mathbb{E}_{w_{x}}[\log(1-\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{C}(w_{x})))]\Big).

(2) Here, 𝒟 \mathcal{D} is optimized to discriminate X X from Y Y using the common codes, whereas H cs H_{\mathrm{cs}} is optimized adversarially so that 𝒞 ⁡ ( w x ) \mathcal{C}(w_{x}) and 𝒞 ⁡ ( w y ) \mathcal{C}(w_{y}) become indistinguishable. To encourage common–salient statistical independence , we introduce two regressors, ℛ x \mathcal{R}_{x} and ℛ y \mathcal{R}_{y} , that attempt to predict the salient outputs 𝒮 x ​ ( w x ) \mathcal{S}_{x}(w_{x}) and 𝒮 y ​ ( w y ) \mathcal{S}_{y}(w_{y}) from the corresponding common outputs 𝒞 ⁡ ( w x ) \mathcal{C}(w_{x}) and 𝒞 ⁡ ( w y ) \mathcal{C}(w_{y}) , respectively. If the regressors can accurately predict salient output from the common one, this indicates that 𝒞 ⁡ ( w ) \mathcal{C}(w) still contains salient information and the separation is incomplete. We therefore train the separator adversarially against the regressors by minimizing the following objective: ℒ R = min H cs ⁡ max ℛ ⁡ ( CLOSE \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{R}=\min_{H_{\mathrm{cs}}}\max_{\mathcal{R}}\Big( − 𝔼 w x [ ∥ ℛ x ( 𝒞 ( w x ) ) − 𝒮 x ( w x ) ∥ 2 2 ] − 𝔼 w y [ ∥ ℛ x ( 𝒞 ( w y ) ) ] \displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{w_{x}}\!\big[\|\mathcal{R}_{x}(\mathcal{C}(w_{x}))\!-\!\mathcal{S}_{x}(w_{x})\|_{2}^{2}\big]\!-\mathbb{E}_{w_{y}}\!\big[\|\mathcal{R}_{x}(\mathcal{C}(w_{y}))\big] (3) − 𝔼 w y [ ∥ ℛ y ( 𝒞 ( w y ) ) − 𝒮 y ( w y ) ∥ 2 2 ] − 𝔼 w x [ ∥ ℛ y ( 𝒞 ( w x ) ) ] ) . \displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{w_{y}}\!\big[\|\mathcal{R}_{y}(\mathcal{C}(w_{y}))\!-\!\mathcal{S}_{y}(w_{y})\|_{2}^{2}\big]\!-\mathbb{E}_{w_{x}}\!\big[\|\mathcal{R}_{y}(\mathcal{C}(w_{x}))\big]\Big). This discourages 𝒞 ⁡ ( w ) \mathcal{C}(w) from encoding salient patterns. We regress s s from c c because c c is typically bigger (more information) and thus tends to absorb s s . Image-Space Losses. We adopt an image-space reconstruction loss combining pixel and perceptual terms.

Given a real image i i and its reconstruction i ^ \widehat{i} , we use ℒ rec ​ ( i , i ^ ) = ‖ i − i ^ ‖ 2 2 + ‖ V ⁡ ( i ) − V ⁡ ( i ^ ) ‖ 2 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}(i,\hat{i})=\|i-\hat{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\|V(i)-V(\hat{i})\|_{2}^{2} , where the first term is a pixel-wise ℓ 2 \ell_{2} loss, and the second term is the LPIPS perceptual loss [ 37 ] . The function V ⁡ ( ⋅ ) V(\cdot) extracts perceptual features using a pretrained VGG16 network [ 31 ] . We use this Eq. to reconstruct both x x and y y , minimizing the image-space loss: ℒ img = ℒ rec ​ ( x , G ⁡ ( c x + s x ) ) + ℒ rec ​ ( y , G ⁡ ( c y + s y ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{img}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}(x,G(c_{x}+s_{x}))+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}(y,G(c_{y}+s_{y})), (4) where G G is the pretrained StyleGAN2 generator. The final loss to train H c ​ s H_{cs} is: ℒ H c ​ s = λ l ​ a ​ t ​ ℒ lat + λ D ​ ℒ D + λ R ​ ℒ R + λ i ​ m ​ g ​ ℒ img \mathcal{L}_{H_{cs}}=\lambda_{lat}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lat}}+\lambda_{D}\mathcal{L}_{D}+\lambda_{R}\mathcal{L}_{R}+\lambda_{img}\mathcal{L}_{\text{img}} (5) F-space Refinement. We first learn common and salient factors in the W W space of StyleGAN2. Then, we add a refinement module that edits intermediate StyleGAN feature space (F space), as in [ 5 ] . Let f ⁡ ( ⋅ ) f(\cdot) denote an intermediate feature of the generator G G , e.g., the output of layer l = 9 l{=}9 . Given the learned latent factors, we define F-space feature shifts for the two swap directions as: Δ ​ f x → y = f ⁡ ( c x + s x ) − f ⁡ ( c x + s y ) ; Δ ​ f y → x = f ⁡ ( c y + s y ) − f ⁡ ( c y + s x ) . \Delta f_{x\rightarrow y}=f(c_{x}+s_{x})-f(c_{x}+s_{y});\;\;\Delta f_{y\rightarrow x}=f(c_{y}+s_{y})-f(c_{y}+s_{x}). (6) Intuitively, Δ ​ f x → y \Delta f_{x\rightarrow y} captures the change induced by replacing the salient factor of x x with the one of y y while keeping c x c_{x} fixed, and Δ ​ f y → x \Delta f_{y\rightarrow x} is defined analogously.

To condition the shifts on the source image, we extract features from reconstructions using a pretrained F-space encoder E f E_{f} : f x = E f ​ ( G ⁡ ( c x + s x ) ) f_{x}\!=\!E_{f}(G(c_{x}\!+\!s_{x})) and f y = E f ​ ( G ⁡ ( c y + s y ) ) f_{y}\!=\!E_{f}(G(c_{y}\!+\!s_{y})) . As in [ 5 ] , we concatenate f f and Δ ​ f \Delta f , and pass them to an adapter F Adpt F_{\text{Adpt}} , yielding: f ^ x → y = F Adpt ​ ( f x ⊕ Δ ​ f x → y ) \widehat{f}_{x\!\rightarrow\!y}\!=\!F_{\text{Adpt}}(f_{x}\!\oplus\!\Delta f_{x\!\rightarrow\!y}) and f ^ y → x = F Adpt ​ ( f y ⊕ Δ ​ f y → x ) \widehat{f}_{y\!\rightarrow\!x}\!=\!F_{\text{Adpt}}(f_{y}\!\oplus\!\Delta f_{y\!\rightarrow\!x}) , where ⊕ \oplus denotes concatenation. Decoding the adapted features with G G yields the edited images. F Adpt F_{\text{Adpt}} is trained with: ℒ x → y = ℒ rec ​ ( G ⁡ ( c x + s y ) , G ⁡ ( f ^ x → y ) ) \mathcal{L}_{x\rightarrow y}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}(G(c_{x}+s_{y}),\;G(\widehat{f}_{x\rightarrow y})) and ℒ y → x = ℒ rec ​ ( G ⁡ ( c y + s x ) , G ⁡ ( f ^ y → x ) ) \mathcal{L}_{y\rightarrow x}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}(G(c_{y}+s_{x}),\;G(\widehat{f}_{y\rightarrow x})) . Finally, we encourage realism with an adversarial loss ℒ adv = ℒ adv- ​ x + ℒ adv- ​ y \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{adv-}x}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{adv-}y} , where ℒ adv- ​ x \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv-}x} is applied to G ⁡ ( f ^ y → x ) G(\widehat{f}_{y\rightarrow x}) against x x , and ℒ adv- ​ y \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv-}y} to G ⁡ ( f ^ x → y ) G(\widehat{f}_{x\rightarrow y}) against y y .

The overall refinement objective is: ℒ refine = ℒ x → y + ℒ y → x + ℒ real + λ a ​ d ​ v ​ ℒ a ​ d ​ v \mathcal{L}_{\text{refine}}=\mathcal{L}_{x\rightarrow y}+\mathcal{L}_{y\rightarrow x}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{real}}+\lambda_{adv}\mathcal{L}_{adv} . 3 Experiments Datasets. We evaluate our method on three 2D medical imaging datasets: BloodMNIST [ 36 ] (Eosinophil Vs Neutrophil; Train=2500/Test=500), OCTMNIST [ 36 ] (Normal Vs Choroidal neovascularization; Train=17000/Test=3000 + Diabetic macular edema Vs Drusen; Train=7000/Test=2000), and BraTS2023 [ 24 ] (Healthy Vs Tumor; Train=8000/Test=2000). For each dataset, we define two groups, denoted X X and Y Y , based on the provided labels. We construct balanced splits such that X X and Y Y contain the same number of images in both training and test sets. All images are preprocessed to a resolution of 256 × 256 256\times 256 . For BloodMNIST and OCTMNIST, we resize the 224 × 224 224\times 224 images from the MedMNIST+ release to 256 × 256 256\times 256 . For MRI scans, we use zero-padding to obtain 256 × 256 256\times 256 images while preserving the original aspect ratio. Implementation Details. We train the proposed CS-StyleGAN in two stages. In Stage 1 , we optimize the separator H cs H_{\mathrm{cs}} to disentangle common and salient factors in the 𝒲 + \mathcal{W}^{+} space. We first warm up H cs H_{\mathrm{cs}} for 2,000 steps using only ℒ lat \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{lat}} and ℒ img \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{img}} to obtain informative latent factors. We then alternate between updating 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and ℛ \mathcal{R} and updating H cs H_{\mathrm{cs}} : with H cs H_{\mathrm{cs}} fixed, 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and ℛ \mathcal{R} are updated by maximizing the objectives in Eqs. ( 2 )–( 3 ) using separate Adam optimizers with a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} ; with 𝒟 \mathcal{D} and ℛ \mathcal{R} fixed, H cs H_{\mathrm{cs}} is updated by minimizing Eq. ( 5 ) using an Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} .

In Stage 2 , using the common and salient factors learned in Stage 1 and their corresponding F-space feature shifts, we optimize the refinement module ( F Adpt F_{\mathrm{Adpt}} ) with ℒ refine \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{refine}} . We use the Ranger optimizer employed in SFE [ 5 ] , with our learning rate set to 10 − 4 10^{-4} . For each dataset, the pSp encoder E E , StyleGAN2 generator G G , and F-space encoder E f E_{f} are pretrained on the corresponding training set before the two-stage training procedure. Detailed network architectures are provided in the supplementary material. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/BioMedTP/CF_Contrastive_Analysis . Baselines and Evaluation Metrics. We compare our method with CA baselines MM-cVAE [ 34 ] , SepVAE [ 23 ] , and Double InfoGAN [ 7 ] , and with diffusion-based VCE methods: ACE [ 15 ] , DiME [ 14 ] , FastDiME [ 35 ] , and TIME [ 16 ] . We also consider off-the-shelf T2I DMs as CF alternatives (not CF-specific methods), including FLUX [ 4 ] and SDXL [ 25 ] adapted with LoRA [ 12 ] . We evaluate the proposed method on CA and CF generation using widely adopted metrics to evaluate synthesis quality: L2, LPIPS [ 37 ] , MS-SSIM [ 33 ] , and FID [ 11 ] . Furthermore, we assess whether swapped outputs match the post-edit domain distribution using FID, reporting FID X → Y {}_{X\!\to\!Y} (FID between X X images after swapping to Y Y and real Y Y ) and FID Y → X {}_{Y\!\to\!X} (swapped Y Y vs. real X X ). We evaluate editing success using the same U-Net-based classifier architecture as in [ 35 ] , trained on real images from the corresponding training set. We report the classification accuracy with respect to the desired post-edit label. About latent separation quality, we train a classifier on the learned latent factors to predict the class ( X X or Y Y ). Higher accuracy indicates the class is encoded in the corresponding (common or salient) space.

Please note that in the BT assumption, the information about X X is entirely encoded in c c . Eventually, following VCE prior works [ 35 , 15 ] , we report FID, sFID, Flip Ratio (FR), Mean Absolute Difference (MAD) and Bidirectional KL Divergence (BKL) for measuring counterfactual quality. Fig. 2 qualitatively compares our method with CA baselines for reconstruction and salient swapping. Our reconstructions are sharper and better preserve fine anatomical structures. For salient swapping, our approach transfers the salient pattern (tumors in BraTS, eosinophil–neutrophil staining differences in BloodMNIST, and CNV-related abnormalities in OCTMNIST) while preserving shared anatomy (healthy brain tissues, global cell layout/nuclear morphology, and normal retinal layer structure, respectively). Table 1 reports quantitative results, where our pSp-based method, with or without F-space refinement ( -Ref ), consistently outperforms all CA baselines on both reconstruction and swapping. Notably, with the MS setting, our method better handles the challenging DME vs.

Drusen case, achieving the best reconstruction metrics and the highest swapping quality (FID and classification accuracy of 0.876). Finally, Table 3 evaluates latent separation between the learned common ( C C ) and salient ( S S ) factors. Salient patterns are mainly captured in S S rather than in C C , and our method attains the lowest separation gap Δ \Delta across all methods, indicating improved semantic disentanglement over prior approaches. Table 4 reports quantitative comparisons on BraTS Healthy ( X X ) and Tumored ( Y Y ) for two counterfactual directions: adding tumors ( X → Y X\!\rightarrow\!Y ) and removing tumors ( Y → X Y\!\rightarrow\!X ).

Overall, our CA-based swapping achieves the best image fidelity in both directions, as indicated by the lowest FID/sFID scores, and is better or on par with diffusion-based CF baselines (ACE, DiME, and FastDiME) in terms of counterfactual effectiveness (i.e., FR/MAD/BKL). In Fig. 3 , we observe that diffusion-based methods struggle to completely remove large tumors from Y Y images, and the added tumors in X → Y X\!\rightarrow\!Y have often limited size and/or are misplaced. In addition, text-conditioned editing (e.g., FLUX) or learning per-image embeddings (e.g., TIME) can drift away from the real image manifold, while fine-tuning large diffusion models with LoRA (e.g., SDXL-LoRA) may alter common content beyond the desired tumor-related changes. By contrast, our approach explicitly swaps salient generative factors between X X and Y Y , improving image fidelity and offering better controllability for tumor-specific counterfactual manipulation. Thanks to the well structured latent space of StyleGAN2, we can also interpolate between salient factors. Given a pair of samples ( x , y ) (x,y) from two domains/classes, we can generate a continuous counterfactual trajectory by scaling the salient change with a scalar α ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha\in[0,1] , e.g., G ⁡ ( α ​ f ^ x → y ) G(\alpha\widehat{f}_{x\rightarrow y}) . This is shown in Fig. 4 , where the predicted class probability changes smoothly along the trajectory, suggesting that the generated counterfactuals form a coherent explanation path. The classifier prediction changes consistently along the trajectory, illustrating gradual insertion/removal of class-specific evidence while preserving common content. 4 Conclusion We propose a classifier-free, CA-based framework for VCEs that yields strong common–salient disentanglement and high-quality CF generations. Interesting perspectives might be adapting the proposed method to recent VLM, as in [ 18 ] , and studying its identifiability. Similarly to all recent VCE [ 14 , 15 , 35 ] and CA [ 7 , 22 ] works, we note that also our method also, without strong assumptions, is not identifiable [ 13 , 21 ] and does not enable causal discovery. This is generally impossible from purely observational single-modal data. An interesting direction, in line with causal representation learning theory [ 29 ] , would be using additional prior or longitudinal data, to further constrain the learning process. 5 Architecture Details 5.1 CS Separator As described in Section 2 , the CS separator H cs , ϕ H_{\mathrm{cs},\phi} contains one common branch and one or two salient branches, depending on the contrastive analysis setting. In the background–target (BT) setting, it consists of the common branch C ϕ c C_{\phi_{c}} and the salient branch S y , ϕ s y S_{y,\phi_{s_{y}}} . In the multiple-salient (MS) setting, an additional salient branch S x , ϕ s x S_{x,\phi_{s_{x}}} is introduced to capture features specific to dataset X X . All branches share the same architecture but have independent parameters. Following He et al. [ 10 ] , we implement each branch as an MLP adapted from StyleGAN2’s 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} -to- 𝒲 \mathcal{W} mapping network [ 17 ] . Each branch comprises four linear layers with equalized learning-rate scaling, each followed by a LeakyReLU activation with a negative slope of 0.2 0.2 .

Unlike the original StyleGAN2 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} -to- 𝒲 \mathcal{W} mapping network, in which each linear layer applies a single 512 × 512 512\times 512 weight matrix to a 512-dimensional latent vector, each linear layer in our separator is parameterized by a weight tensor 𝐀 ( k ) ∈ ℝ L × 512 × 512 \mathbf{A}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times 512\times 512} to process the 𝒲 + \mathcal{W}^{+} code w = [ w 1 , … , w L ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ L × 512 w=[w_{1},\ldots,w_{L}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times 512} . Here, k = 1 , … , 4 k=1,\ldots,4 indexes the linear layer, and L L denotes the number of style vectors in the 𝒲 + \mathcal{W}^{+} code. For a generator with a native output resolution of R × R R\times R , L L is given by L = 2 ​ log 2 ⁡ ( R ) − 2 L=2\log_{2}(R)-2 . In our experiments, all StyleGAN2 generators are pretrained at a native resolution of 256 × 256 256\times 256 , yielding L = 14 L=14 . This design assigns a position-specific weight matrix to each style position. Since each layer preserves the dimensionality of the latent code, it maps from ℝ B × L × 512 \mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times 512} to ℝ B × L × 512 \mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times 512} , where B B denotes the batch size. 5.2 Regularization Networks D D and R R As described in Section 2 , we employ a domain discriminator D D and a dependency regressor R R to regularize the common and salient representations. Given a common representation c ∈ ℝ L × 512 c\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times 512} , the domain discriminator first flattens the complete representation into a single vector. Since our StyleGAN2 generator operates at a native resolution of 256 × 256 256\times 256 , we have L = 14 L=14 , resulting in a 7168-dimensional input vector. The discriminator is implemented as a binary linear classifier with a single fully connected layer mapping the 7168-dimensional input to one output logit. No hidden layer or output activation is used, and the network directly produces a single domain-classification logit.

The dependency regressor R R predicts the salient representation from the corresponding common representation. Given a batch of common representations c ∈ ℝ B × L × 512 c\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times 512} , the batch and style dimensions are merged to form a matrix in ℝ ( B ​ L ) × 512 \mathbb{R}^{(BL)\times 512} . The regressor consists of two fully connected layers that map this matrix from ( B ​ L ) × 512 (BL)\times 512 to ( B ​ L ) × 512 (BL)\times 512 , with a ReLU activation between the two layers and no activation after the output layer. The output is then reshaped back to obtain the predicted salient factor s ^ ∈ ℝ B × L × 512 \hat{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times 512} . 5.3 Other Architectures and Implementations For the remaining network components, we use the pSp architecture [ 26 ] for E E and the StyleGAN2 architecture [ 17 ] for G G . The F-space refinement stage builds upon SFE [ 5 ] , retaining the original architectures of its F-space encoder E f E_{f} and trainable adapter F Adpt F_{\mathrm{Adpt}} . For the original StyleGAN2 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} -to- 𝒲 \mathcal{W} mapping network on which the separator architecture is based, we refer to the implementation provided at https://nn.labml.ai/gan/stylegan/index.html . For the StyleGAN2 generator G G , we use the PyTorch implementation by rosinality, available at https://github.com/rosinality/stylegan2-pytorch . The same pretrained G G is used throughout both training stages and evaluation. To compute ℒ adv \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}} , we use the discriminator pretrained jointly with G G . For image-level evaluation, we adopt the U-Net-based classifier used in [ 35 ] . The classifier is trained on real images from the corresponding training set and subsequently applied to the edited images to assess whether they exhibit the intended target attributes.

For latent-space evaluation, we quantify the separation between the learned common and salient factors by training a logistic regression classifier to predict the dataset label from each factor. The classifier is implemented in scikit-learn. With only the base reconstruction objectives (W/o Reg.), the swaps produce limited class-specific changes. Adding ℒ D \mathcal{L}_{D} improves tumor removal in the y → x y\rightarrow x direction but not tumor addition in the x → y x\rightarrow y direction. Adding ℒ R \mathcal{L}_{R} improves common–salient separation, enabling clearer bidirectional edits while better preserving the source anatomy. Finally, F-space refinement enhances local details and image fidelity without changing the semantic effect of the edit. These results are consistent with the quantitative ablation in Table 3. Fig. 6 compares the BT and MS assumptions on OCTMNIST. While both variants reconstruct the inputs well, the BT variant produces limited swapping effects because it cannot separately model the class-specific patterns of DME and drusen. The proposed MS variant, with two salient branches, enables more meaningful bidirectional swaps while preserving the common retinal structure.
